name: Fatima Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a 95-hectare farm from the county council, so it's a council tenancy, and I've had it for nine years. We run 400 ewes and grow winter wheat, plus a few beef calves I buy in and fatten. A normal day is the sheep first thing, then whatever field work is due, then paperwork at the kitchen table after the kids are in bed. My partner Tom works part-time at the feed mill in Corrin, and he does the lambing nights with me in spring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you love, and what's the part that grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the first week of lambing, even with no sleep, when the shed fills up and it all works. What grinds me down is the forms: grants, movement records, the council's inspections. I've started using one of those AI chat tools now and then to help word the grant forms, and it saves me an evening, I'll admit that. The other thing is the tenancy. It's up for review in 2031, and the council has sold off two farms near us already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, nothing lost, nothing gained much. The chat tool would still help with grant forms, and the sheep would still need lambing. At the co-op meetings I'd say our real problem is fertiliser prices and the council selling farms, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the tenancy is my worry in every one of these pictures. If the council sells our farm in 2031 to pay for something else, we lose the house and the business in one go. That's true whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as we are and keep using the chat tool for paperwork. I'd go along to the county tenants' group and push them to lobby the council not to sell any more farms. And I'd try to get our savings from about three months up to four before the tenancy review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Life's normal, but I've got this date, 2031, sitting in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing the tenancy actually mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farmhouse comes with the tenancy, so it'd mean moving the kids, maybe out of Amira's school just before her exams. Tom's job is part-time, so we couldn't buy a house round here on that. We'd be starting again in our fifties with a few thousand in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the tenants' group. Do you think the council listens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, if there's enough of us and it gets in the local paper. When they tried to sell Brook Farm two years ago, twenty of us turned up at the council meeting and they backed off for a year. So yes, it's slow, but it's not nothing.

say: Nothing much changes, and our real problem is **fertiliser prices**.
The council **selling farms** matters far more to us than robots do.
think: The **2031 tenancy review** is my worry in every picture.
Losing the tenancy means losing the **house and the business** together.
do: Push the **county tenants' group** to lobby against more farm sales.
Raise savings from **three to four months** before the tenancy review.
Keep using the **chat tool** to word grant forms and save evenings.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the 2031 review date always at the back of my mind.
S0.quote: If the council sells our farm in 2031 to pay for something else, we lose the house and the business in one go.
fieldNote: Fatima's anxiety is about **tenure**, not technology, and it runs through her whole life.
She already uses AI for **paperwork** and finds it saves an evening.
Her instinct is **collective**: tenants' group, council meetings, the local paper.
Her income feels safe now, so the worry stays at **uneasy**.

steps.text: Push the tenants' group to lobby the council against farm sales
Raise savings from three to four months before the 2031 review
Keep lambing 400 ewes and growing wheat as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for small farms if it's shared out properly. If AI does the forms, the ordering and the planning, that's my evenings back. I'd tell people at the co-op we should get one shared system, not everyone paying for their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps me more than it hurts in this one. The thinking bits of farming are the smallest part of my week, and the sheep still need hands. What I'd watch is the council using AI to score tenancies, because a computer looking at yield per hectare will always say merge the small farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the paperwork tools properly, not just now and then, probably on a co-op evening course. I'd push the co-op to buy one shared planning and ordering system for all twenty members. And I'd ask the tenants' group to demand that the council publishes how any AI scoring of farms works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit wary. It's like a new tractor salesman: helpful, but I'd still count my fingers after shaking hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the council might use AI to score tenancies. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A program looks at yield per hectare and decides 95 hectares is too small to be worth keeping. It wouldn't see that we've built up the soil and the hedges for nine years. That's why I'd want a person, not a program, making the final call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bit of the paperwork would you hand over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sheep movement records and the grant applications, without a second thought. Those take me six or seven hours a month. I'd spend that time with Sam at football instead of swearing at a form.

say: This helps **small farms** if it's shared out properly.
The co-op should buy **one shared system** instead of everyone paying alone.
think: The **thinking work** is the smallest part of my week, so this helps me.
The risk is the council using **AI scoring** that favours merging small farms.
do: Learn the **paperwork tools** properly on a co-op evening course.
Push the co-op to buy a **shared planning system** for twenty members.
Ask the tenants' group to demand the council publishes **how AI scoring** works.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but wary of who controls the new tools.
S1.quote: A computer looking at yield per hectare will always say merge the small farms.
fieldNote: Fatima sees Steady Disruption as mostly **useful** for a small hands-on farm.
Her real fear moves to **who controls** the AI: the council, not her.
She thinks in **shared** terms, wanting a co-op system rather than buying alone.
Her steady approach shows: learn properly once it's **proven useful**.

steps.text: Take a co-op evening course on farm paperwork tools
Push the co-op to buy one shared planning and ordering system
Keep running the ewes and wheat with the same hands-on routine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in now, with rules on who owns the robots and who gets the money. I'd be online for once, sharing everything the tenant farmers' groups put out. Public land like council farms should be used to keep families on the land, not handed to whoever has the most machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the timing is awful for us. Our tenancy review lands in 2031, the same year the robots arrive, and the council will be looking at a company offering to run ten farms with machines. I think we'd lose the farm, and I think the tenancy is the weak point, not my skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get the tenants' group and the co-op to put a joint proposal to the council: let us bid together for shared robots and keep the tenancies. I'd write to every councillor and our national representative asking for public land to stay in family hands. At home we'd stop the kitchen extension we'd saved for and keep that 6,000 as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. It's the feeling you get when you see a ewe on her back and you're three fields away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking work changes in 2028 and the robots come about three years later. How do you use those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 my paperwork vanishes, which I wouldn't mind, but so does the council's need for a land agent to visit us. Those three years are for organising, because once the robots are here it's too late to argue. If we haven't got a deal by 2030, I'd be looking for a house to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth in small doses, because kids know when you're hiding something. I'd say we might move, and that their dad and I would make sure they finish school where they are. Amira would want to fight it with me, she's that age.

say: Governments must set **rules on robot ownership** and who gets the money.
Council farms should keep **families on the land**, not go to the biggest machine owner.
think: Our **2031 tenancy review** lands the same year the robots arrive.
I expect to **lose the farm**, because the tenancy is our weak point.
do: Put a **joint co-op bid** for shared robots to the council this year.
Write to every **councillor** asking that public land stays with families.
Stop the kitchen extension and keep the **6,000** as a cushion.
feel: **Sick and helpless**, like seeing a sheep in trouble three fields away.
S2.quote: Our tenancy review lands in 2031, the same year the robots arrive, and the council will be looking at a company offering to run ten farms with machines.
fieldNote: Fatima expects to **lose farm and home** because of when her tenancy ends.
She treats the three-year gap as an **organising window** before robots arrive.
Her plan mixes **co-op bidding** and political pressure on the council.
She would tell her children the truth in **small doses**.

steps.text: Put a joint co-op bid for shared robots to the council
Write to every councillor about keeping council farms with families
Shelve the kitchen extension and keep the 6,000 saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if the council and the co-ops start talking today. I'd be at the co-op meeting saying let's not wait for the council to decide for us. Small farms can share robots the way we share a combine harvester now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd have a fighting chance in this one. The tenancy review is in 2031 when AGI lands, but the robots don't come until 2034, so the council would still need people on the farms at the review. If we've got a shared robot plan by then, we look like the future, not the past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put 2,000 into the co-op's machinery fund toward a shared share in field robots once they're proven. I'd learn the planning software properly in 2027 so I'm comfortable before AGI arrives. And I'd lead the tenants' group pitch to the council for a new ten-year tenancy tied to the shared robot plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a working way. It's like the week before lambing: a lot could go wrong, but I know what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put 2,000 into the co-op. Is that money you can spare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it's about a month of our cushion. But a share in a robot I can use is worth more than a month in the bank if it keeps the tenancy. Tom and I would argue about it for a week and then do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your own work once the robots arrive in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be the one running the sheep with the robots doing the heavy, boring stuff, like fencing and carting feed. I'd still want to do lambing by hand, at least the hard births. My income might drop a bit, but I'd still be a farmer, which is the point.

say: Five years is enough if **councils and co-ops** start talking today.
Small farms can **share robots** the way we share a combine now.
think: The robots arrive **after the tenancy review**, which gives us a fighting chance.
A **shared robot plan** makes us look like the future, not the past.
do: Put **2,000** into the co-op machinery fund for shared field robots.
Learn the **planning software** properly in 2027, before AGI arrives.
Lead the tenants' pitch for a **new ten-year tenancy** tied to the plan.
feel: **Nervous but busy**, like the week before lambing.
S3.quote: Small farms can share robots the way we share a combine harvester now.
fieldNote: The extra time turns Fatima's fear into a **working plan** around the tenancy.
She's ready to risk **a month of savings** on a co-op robot share.
She expects her **income could dip**, keeping her anxious despite the plan.
She wants to keep the **hard lambing** work by hand.

steps.text: Put 2,000 into the co-op machinery fund for shared robots
Learn the farm planning software properly during 2027
Lead the tenants' pitch for a ten-year tenancy with robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want the national farmers' groups pushing for public money to help small farms buy into robots together. If it's done right, robots could be the thing that saves small farms instead of killing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right in this one. The tenancy review in 2031 comes before AGI, so we'd likely get another ten years. By 2039 I'd be 56, the kids would be grown, and the co-op would have had years to sort out shared robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd mostly carry on, and keep using AI for forms now and then. I'd get the co-op to set up a small robot working group that visits trial farms once a year. And I'd keep saving steadily, aiming for six months of cushion by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. There's a worry about the country more than about us, about people in jobs with less time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said calm, but you've also been worried about the tenancy in every picture. Which is it here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tenancy is still the thing, it always is. But in this picture the review comes before anything big happens, so I'd go into it with a clean record and no robot company bidding against us. That's why it's on my mind but not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if not yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, a bit, because the feed mill's office could go once AI handles orders. And my sister Nadia, who works in a call centre in town. Her job's all thinking work and AI arrives in 2036 whatever we do.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, and wasting it would be foolish.
Public money for **shared robots** could save small farms.
think: The tenancy review comes **before AGI**, so we'd likely get ten more years.
By 2039 I'd be 56 with **grown kids** and a co-op robot plan.
do: Carry on farming and use **AI tools** for forms now and then.
Set up a co-op **robot working group** that visits trial farms yearly.
Save steadily toward **six months** of cushion by 2031.
feel: **Fairly calm** about us, but worried for people in desk jobs.
S4.quote: If it's done right, robots could be the thing that saves small farms instead of killing them.
fieldNote: Fatima's mood depends on **timing**: here the tenancy review comes first.
Her concern shifts to **Tom's mill job** and her sister's call centre work.
She still thinks **collectively**, wanting co-op groups and public money.
She admits the tenancy is always **on her mind**, so she isn't fully calm.

steps.text: Keep farming and use AI tools for forms now and then
Set up a co-op robot working group that visits trial farms
Save toward six months of cushion before the 2031 review

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the date. The robots arrive the same year our tenancy is reviewed, and that's the one where I lose the house as well as the farm. What would help is a council promise that tenants get first chance to adopt robots together before any farm is merged or sold.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people where they live, not just where they work. For tenant farmers the house and the job are the same thing, and a change in one takes the other with it.

headlineQuote: For tenant farmers the house and the job are the same thing, and a change in one takes the other with it.
portrait: Fatima Walsh is a **43-year-old council tenant** farming 400 ewes and wheat, with a partner and two kids.
Her worry in every picture is the **2031 tenancy review**, because the farmhouse comes with the farm.
She uses AI **now and then** for forms and sees Steady Disruption as mostly helpful.
In the AGI pictures she turns to **co-ops and councils**, wanting shared robots for small farms.
Her mood follows **timing**: worst when robots and the tenancy review land together.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive the same year as her tenancy review.
whatWouldHelp: A **council promise** that tenants can adopt robots together before any farm is merged or sold.
